# Appeal of Denial — Partial Knee Replacement (CPT 27446)

**RE:** Appeal of Adverse Benefit Determination, Reference #POC-EED29F7594-68772
**Member:** Morgan Foster
**Member ID:** W276906709
**Date of Denial Notice:** 2026-08-11
**Plan:** Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield (Commercial/ACA), Kentucky
**Governing Policy Cited by Plan:** Carelon Joint Surgery (MSK02-1125.1) — https://guidelines.carelonmedicalbenefitsmanagement.com/joint-surgery-2025-11-15/ (effective 2025-11-15)

Dear Appeals Reviewer,

I am appealing the denial of my prior authorization request for a partial knee replacement (CPT 27446). My surgeon, Dr. Lindqvist, has documented that this procedure is medically necessary, and I am asking the plan to reconsider its decision.

## Why I am appealing

The denial notice states that "the imaging findings submitted do not support the medical necessity of the requested procedure." I want to address this directly, but I also want to flag an important problem with the materials I received.

**The criteria the plan sent to support this denial do not appear to apply to my procedure.** The policy excerpts provided to me under the title "Carelon Joint Surgery (MSK02-1125.1)" all address *shoulder* arthroplasty, hemiarthroplasty, reverse shoulder arthroplasty, and revision of a *shoulder* prosthesis — for example, criteria involving "the glenohumeral joint," "the humeral head," and "the glenoid." My procedure is a **partial knee replacement**, not a shoulder procedure. I have not been given the specific section of this policy (or any other policy) that sets out the medically necessary indications for partial knee replacement, so I am not able to show point-by-point how my records meet knee-specific criteria — because I have not been shown what those criteria are. I am asking the plan to identify and apply the correct criteria for CPT 27446 and to explain, referencing that specific language, why my records do not meet it.

In the meantime, I want to lay out the clinical facts that are already in my file, because they speak directly to the medical necessity of this surgery:

- **Duration and severity of symptoms:** I have had 14 months of progressive knee pain that has not improved with rest.
- **Conservative treatment already tried and failed:** I completed 16 weeks of supervised physical therapy (24 visits, 2026-02-25 to 2026-06-17) focused on strengthening and range of motion, as documented in my physical therapy discharge note. I also used NSAIDs for 4 months without adequate relief, and had a corticosteroid injection on 2026-03-26 that gave only 2 weeks of partial relief.
- **Imaging findings:** An MRI of my knee on 2026-06-27 showed full-thickness cartilage loss in the medial compartment with bone-on-bone contact, and Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4 changes medially. This is the imaging the denial says does not support medical necessity, but it documents severe, end-stage degenerative joint disease.
- **Functional impact:** I cannot climb stairs without assistance, and I wake 3–4 times a night because of pain.
- **Exam findings:** My physical exam showed positive provocative testing on the affected side and range of motion limited by pain.
- **No contraindications:** I have no active infection, no untreated substance use, a BMI of 29, and I do not smoke.

I recognize the citations I was given describe a *shoulder* policy's requirement that, for example, medical necessity can be shown by "Pain and loss of function of at least 6 months' duration that interferes with daily activities (unless radiographs show Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4)" and by "Radiographic evidence of destructive degenerative joint disease as evidenced by marked joint space narrowing." I note this only because the pattern of findings in my own knee — 14 months of pain interfering with daily activities, Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4 changes, and marked joint space narrowing with bone-on-bone apposition — is the same type of severe, well-documented degenerative disease that this kind of medical policy is generally written to address, even though these particular quoted sentences govern the shoulder, not the knee.

## What I am asking for

1. That the plan reconsider the denial of CPT 27446 in light of the clinical record above.
2. That the plan identify the specific medical policy and criteria that actually apply to partial knee replacement (CPT 27446), since the excerpts I received govern shoulder arthroplasty and do not appear to be the correct authority for this denial.
3. That the plan provide a written response addressing how my documented imaging, conservative treatment history, and functional limitations relate to the correct, applicable criteria.

I understand this appeal must be received by 2027-02-07, and I am submitting it well before that deadline. I will send this appeal to the address printed on my denial letter, and I am also available to submit it through anthem.com, the Sydney Health app, or by calling the number on my member ID card if that is preferred.

Thank you for reconsidering my request. Please let me know if any additional records from Dr. Lindqvist or my physical therapy provider would help with this review.

Sincerely,

[Morgan Foster]
[Address]
[Phone number]
[Email address]
Member ID: W276906709

---

*This letter is not medical or legal advice and does not guarantee that coverage will be approved.*

quotes: shoulder arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for ANY of the following indications:

Limited range of motion or crepitus of the glenohumeral joint on physical examination Pain and loss of function of at least 6 months’ duration that interferes with daily activities (unless radiographs show Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4) *Radiographic evidence of destructive degenerative joint disease as evidenced by marked joint space narrowing AND ONE or more of the following:

Irregular joint surfaces Glenoid sclerosis Osteophyte changes Flattened glenoid Cystic changes in the humeral head Failure of conservative management of at least 6 weeks’ duration (unless radiographs show Kellgren-Lawrence grade 4 or diffuse modified Outerbridge grade III-IV changes) Hemiarthroplasty Hemiarthroplasty is considered medically necessary for ANY of the following indications:

Proximal humerus fracture confirmed by imaging not amenable to internal fixation (e.g., severe comminution, poor bone quality, multi-part, displaced) Malignancy involving the glenohumeral joint or surrounding soft tissue Advanced joint disease of the shoulder when criteria for total shoulder arthroplasty are met AND at least ONE of the following conditions is present:

Osteonecrosis of the humeral head without glenoid involvement Glenoid bone stock inadequate to support a glenoid prosthesis Advanced joint disease due to rotator cuff tear arthropathy* Glenohumeral osteoarthritis with irreparable rotator cuff tear* *except for Exclusions listed below Reverse Shoulder Arthroplasty Reverse shoulder arthroplasty is considered medically necessary for ANY of the following indications:

Deficient rotator cuff with limited ability to actively flex the upper extremity above the plane of the shoulder Revision or Replacement of a Shoulder Prosthesis Revision or replacement of a shoulder prosthesis is considered medically necessary for ANY of the following conditions when associated with pain and functional impairment:
Preoperative investigation using serologic testing and IF there are abnormal laboratory findings, at least ONE of the following:

Synovial fluid testing, such as leukocyte count and neutrophil percentage, aerobic and anaerobic bacterial cultures, leukocyte esterase, alpha defensin testing (Synovasure®), synovial fluid CRP, synovial fluid PCR for bacteria Intraoperative plan for histopathology and/or aerobic and anaerobic tissue cultures using implant sonication for cultures or PCR Contraindications All procedures listed in this guideline are contraindicated when ANY of the following conditions are present:

Active infection of the joint Active systemic bacteremia Active skin infection or open wound at the surgical site Rapidly progressive neurologic disease Intra-articular corticosteroid injection within the past 6 weeks in the joint being replaced Exclusions Indications other than those addressed in this guideline are considered not medically necessary including, but not limited to, the following:

Shoulder arthroplasty under conditions which would result in excessive stress on the implant including, but not limited to, Charcot joint and paralytic conditions of the shoulder Shoulder resurfacing, including total, hemi, or partial resurfacing (e.g., Copeland™, the Extended Articulating Surface (EAS)™ Resurfacing Heads, Global CAP™ CTA Resurfacing Shoulder Humeral Head)
